subject: 5-Bullet Friday — The Real-Life Willy Wonka, Hyper growth Formulas, and Bizarre Films That Inspire

bullets.title: The Real-Life Willy Wonka Who Built Tony Hawk a Secret Desert Train
bullets.note:
on the [_Death, Sex & Money_](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/death-sex-money/id870688022) podcast**.** Hat tip to [Elan Lee](https://www.elanlee.com/) for the great recommendation. N.D., if you see this, Elan would love to meet you, and I think the two of you would really hit it off.  
​  
​_N.D. Austin is not an event planner. He designs experiences, which he says are supposed to leave you feeling transformed. He’s designed hundreds over the years, from secret sewer speakeasies to coming-of-age rituals on deserted islands to funeral board games that guide people through decades of memories. In this episode, host Anna Sale talks to skateboarding legend Tony Hawk about an experience N.D. designed for Tony’s office that mended friendships on a homemade train. And N.D. tells Anna how growing up in a doomsday cult in Alaska sparked his obsession with performance, ritual and generosity._

bullets.title: The Algorithm: The Hypergrowth Formula That Transformed Tesla, Lululemon, General Motors, and SpaceX
bullets.creator: Jon McNeill, former president of Tesla
bullets.note:
This is an incredibly tactical and concise book, and apparently the first such book written by an Elon direct report. The audiobook version clocks in at only 4.5 hours on 1x speed. I made nearly 100 highlights, and I asked my COO to read the book, as we will be emulating parts of the playbook.  
​  
From the description:  
​_Jon McNeill had already founded and sold six startups when Sheryl Sandberg introduced him to Elon Musk, who was looking for help at Tesla. McNeill was steeped in the lean principles that had made Toyota a global powerhouse—principles focused on achieving efficiency and optimization by incrementally improving existing systems and processes. What he learned from Elon at Tesla was its antithesis, an approach that required radical rethinking. … Elon called this five-step framework “The Algorithm.”  
​

bullets.title: One year ago this week, I asked my ~1.9M X followers to make stock and crypto predictions. I promised I’d report back.
bullets.note: The outcome? As of November 3rd, they ranked the stocks 100% correctly and ranked the crypto 100% incorrectly. Read the details and methodology [here](https://x.com/tferriss/status/2118067628317319354).

bullets.title: You Can See Everything
bullets.note:
from [A24](https://a24films.com/), and it blew my mind. It redefines what a documentary can be, partially by creating an IV drip of WTF moments and blurring every line imaginable. It inspired the hell out of me. Editing that film almost certainly took 10 years off of the lives of [Nathan Fielder](https://x.com/nathanfielder), [Lance Oppenheim](https://www.instagram.com/lanceopp/?hl=en), and team. If they’d gone 80%, it would have been terrible. Instead, they went 100%, and it’s a masterpiece. I’ve seen all sorts of buzz online around their “marketing playbook,” but here’s their marketing secret: make the product so ridiculously good and unique that people can’t stop talking about it.  
​  
“Where am I 3/4-assing?” is the question haunting me this week. What a gift. [Watch the trailer here](https://a24films.com/films/you-can-see-everything/video/you-can-see-everything-trailer).

bullets.title: Lucky #888 — My Tour of Designing Luck in China, Japan, and Korea
bullets.note: I did a lot of reading for this short 30-minute episode, which features a nerdy tour of China, Japan, and Korea, including a million-dollar license plate, disappearing hotel floors, a casino room designed around one gambler’s birthday, and the lucky number hiding in Toyota’s name. It’s my excuse to dust off some of my East Asian Studies and indulge a few weird interests. You can listen [here](https://tim.blog/2026/11/05/lucky-888-my-tour-of-designing-luck-in-china-japan-and-korea/?utm_source=convertkit&utm_medium=convertkit&utm_campaign=5bf).

bullets.title: “Happiness is the absence of the striving for happiness.” ― Adapted from Chuang Tzu, one of the founding figures of Daoism. This is the first half of 至樂無樂, 至譽無譽 (Zhì lè wú lè, Zhì yù wú yù), which is decently translated as “Highest happiness \[is\] no happiness; Highest praise/renown \[is\] no praise/renown.” The context in Chapter 18 of Zhuangzi is what makes me comfortable with the above English translation, which I love. Chuang Tzu’s point, as far as I understand it, is that when you empty yourself of the conscious striving to be happy or famous, you achieve something far better. Daoist lè (happiness, joy), rather than being a spike in emotion caused by getting what you want, is a steady undercurrent of contentment. The spiritual cousin of this quote, often misattributed to Nathaniel Hawthorne, actually comes from an anonymous “L.” in a New Orleans newspaper from 1848: “Happiness is a butterfly, which when pursued, seems always just beyond your grasp; but if you sit down quietly, may alight upon you.”
